For each cell, determine if it is a "valid cell" (i.e., its 8 corners contain at least one vertex with value $> p$ and one with value $< p$) [S1].

The claim defines a 'valid cell' as one where its 8 corners contain at least one vertex with value > p and one with value < p. The provided text explains that the Marching Cubes method determines the topology of the isosurface inside a cell based on the function values at the 8 vertices relative to the isovalue p. It states that if all vertices were on the same side of p (all > p or all < p), the isosurface would not pass through the cell, and thus the cell would not be 'valid' (i.e., it would not contribute to the isosurface). Conversely, for the isosurface to intersect the cell (making it valid), the vertices must straddle the isovalue p, meaning there must be at least one vertex with value > p and at least one with value < p. This is the fundamental principle of the Marching Cubes algorithm described in the text.
